# Finding and reading the sources {#sec-finding-sources}

This handbook cites more than a hundred sources: books, research papers,
international standards, Python Enhancement Proposals, official documentation,
and a few blog posts. This appendix explains **what each kind of source is**,
**how to obtain it legally** (very often for free), **how to read it
efficiently**, and **how to check** that a citation is accurate.

## How to read a citation in this book {#sec-reading-citations}

A citation such as @goldberg1991 or [@cormen2022, §16.4] is a link to the
full entry in the [References](../references.qmd). The part after the comma,
when present, says **where** in the source to look (a section, chapter, page
or theorem number). Each entry in the references contains, whenever they
exist:

| Field | Example | What to do with it |
|---|---|---|
| **DOI** | `10.1145/103162.103163` | open `https://doi.org/10.1145/103162.103163`: it always redirects to the publisher's current page |
| **arXiv id** | `2107.03374` | open `https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374`: free full text, with all versions |
| **ISBN** | `978-0-262-04630-5` | the identifier of a book edition; use it in library catalogues and bookshops |
| **URL** | `https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/` | for standards, documentation and web pages |
| **Note** | "Free on the AMS website" | **how to obtain** the source and **which parts** this book uses |

The notes are part of the design of this book: every entry tells you where a
free, legal copy exists, or which library service to use.

## Kinds of sources {#sec-kinds-of-sources}

### Books

Textbooks such as @knuth1997, @cormen2022 or @higham2002 are the most
reliable sources: they are long-lived, carefully edited and self-contained.

- **Editions matter**: section numbers change between editions. This book
  always gives the edition in the entry (e.g. CLRS **4th** edition, 2022).
- **Free legal copies**: some classics are free online from their publishers
  or authors (e.g. @abelson1996, @mckinney2022); works in the **public domain**
  (e.g. @boole1854) are on Project Gutenberg and the Internet Archive.
- **Libraries**: university libraries give access to most of the others, often
  as e-books. Public libraries offer interlibrary loan.
- Avoid unauthorised copies: besides the legal issue, they are frequently the
  wrong edition.

### Research papers

A **journal article** or **conference paper** reports original results after
**peer review**. A **preprint** is the authors' version made public before or
during review, typically on **arXiv** (<https://arxiv.org>) for mathematics,
computer science and physics. In machine learning many influential papers are
read primarily on arXiv (e.g. @vaswani2017, @chen2021).

How to get the full text:

1. Open the **DOI** link: many papers are **open access**.
2. Search the title on **arXiv**, **Google Scholar** (click *"All N
   versions"* to find free copies) or **Semantic Scholar**.
3. Use the **Unpaywall** browser extension, which finds legal free versions
   automatically.
4. Look at the **authors' home pages**: many post their papers.
5. Use your **university library** (proxy or VPN), which pays for
   subscriptions.
6. Write to the authors: they are usually glad to send a copy.

When a preprint and a published version both exist, cite the **published**
version (it has been reviewed), but feel free to *read* the preprint. Check
that you are reading the latest arXiv version (`v1`, `v2`, … appear in the
page's history).

### Standards and specifications

Standards define formats and protocols precisely; they are the ultimate
authority on *what is correct*.

| Body | Examples in this book | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **IETF** (RFCs) | @rfc3629 (UTF-8), @rfc4180 (CSV), @rfc8259 (JSON) | free at <https://www.rfc-editor.org> |
| **W3C** | @png2003 (PNG) | free |
| **The Open Group / IEEE** (POSIX) | @posixrename, @posixtime | free online edition |
| **Unicode Consortium** | @unicode | free |
| **ITU-T** | @itue164 | free download |
| **IEEE** | @ieee754 | paywalled; through libraries |
| **ISO** | @iso8601 | paywalled; often a free equivalent exists (e.g. RFC 3339 for dates) |

Reading a standard is a skill: start from the table of contents, read the
*terminology* and *conformance* sections, and look for the normative keywords
**MUST**, **SHOULD**, **MAY**, whose meaning is itself standardised (RFC 2119).

### Python Enhancement Proposals (PEPs)

A **PEP** is a design document proposing a change to Python or describing a
process [@pep1]. Each has a number, authors, a **status** (*Draft*,
*Accepted*, *Final*, *Rejected*, *Superseded*…) and a creation date. PEPs are
the best source for **why** Python works the way it does: each contains a
*Motivation* and a *Rationale* section, often with rejected alternatives. Read
them at <https://peps.python.org>. Once a feature ships, the **documentation**
(below) becomes the normative reference and some PEPs carry a banner pointing
to it.

### Official documentation

The Python documentation (<https://docs.python.org>) has several parts with
different purposes:

| Part | Purpose | Cited as |
|---|---|---|
| **Tutorial** | a guided introduction | @pythontutorial |
| **Library Reference** | every built-in and standard module | @pythonlibrary |
| **Language Reference** | the exact syntax and semantics | @pythonreference |
| **HOWTOs** | in-depth guides (sorting, logging, descriptors, MRO…) | e.g. @simionato2003 |
| **Glossary** | definitions of terms (EAFP, iterable, hashable…) | — |

Always select the **version** matching your interpreter (drop-down menu at the
top of each page): behaviour changes between versions, as we saw with
`sum()` in Python 3.12 (@sec-math-module). The same applies to third-party
libraries (NumPy, pandas, …) and to packaging (@ppug).

### Blogs, mailing lists, social media

A few sources in this book are blog posts or messages (e.g. @hettinger2012,
@cox2016, @karpathy2025). They are cited when they are the **primary**
source of an idea or a term. Treat them as primary evidence of *who said what
and when*, not as peer-reviewed results. Web pages can change or disappear:
the **Internet Archive's Wayback Machine** (<https://web.archive.org>) keeps
snapshots; paste the URL there if a link is broken.

## How to read a paper efficiently {#sec-how-to-read-a-paper}

S. Keshav's **three-pass method** [@keshav2007] is a good default:

1. **First pass (5–10 minutes)**: title, abstract, introduction, section
   headings, conclusions, a glance at the references. Goal: *what is the
   problem, what is the claim, is it relevant to me?*
2. **Second pass (about an hour)**: read the paper but skip the proofs;
   study figures, tables and the main equations; note what you do not
   understand. Goal: *being able to summarise the contribution and the
   evidence to someone else.*
3. **Third pass (several hours)**: *re-derive* the paper — redo the proofs
   and the experiments in your head (or in code), questioning every
   assumption. This is what the "For the interested reader" boxes of this book
   invite you to do.

For mathematical texts, read with **pencil and paper**: after each definition
write an example and a non-example; after each theorem, try to find why each
hypothesis is needed.

## How to verify a citation {#sec-verify-citation}

Citations can be wrong — by mistake, through "citation chains" where a claim
is copied without checking the original, or because an AI tool **invented**
them (language models can produce plausible but non-existent references;
@sec-ch-ai-tools). Checklist:

1. **Resolve the identifier**: the DOI or arXiv id must open the right
   document (same title, authors, year).
2. **Find the exact place**: the section or page cited must actually contain
   the claim.
3. **Prefer the primary source**: if a textbook says "Lamé proved…", the
   primary source is @lame1844; cite both when you used both.
4. **Check status**: has the paper been **retracted** or corrected (the
   publisher's page and the Retraction Watch database say so)? Has the PEP been
   superseded? Is the documentation for your version?
5. **Check numbers against the source**: percentages and dates are the
   most frequently corrupted details (e.g. this book cross-checked the figures
   of @peng2023, @becker2025, @pearce2022 and @spracklen2025 against the
   original papers).

## Building your own bibliography {#sec-own-bibliography}

- Use a reference manager such as **Zotero** (free and open source): it
  captures references from web pages with one click, stores PDFs, and exports
  BibTeX.
- Any DOI can be converted to a BibTeX entry automatically through
  **content negotiation**:

```bash
curl -LH "Accept: application/x-bibtex" https://doi.org/10.1145/361598.361623
```

- arXiv pages have an *"Export BibTeX citation"* link; Google Scholar has a
  *"Cite → BibTeX"* button (check its output: it is often incomplete).

### How the bibliography of this book is organised

The file `references.bib` in the repository is plain BibTeX, rendered by
Quarto in the [References](../references.qmd) with the Chicago author–date
style. Its conventions are:

- keys are `firstauthorYEAR` (plus a suffix when needed: `knuth1997b`);
- entries are grouped by part and chapter, in the order they are first used;
- every entry carries a DOI, arXiv id, ISBN or URL when one exists, and a
  `note` saying how to obtain it and which parts are used;
- PEPs, RFCs and documentation pages are entries like any other, so that every
  claim in the text can be traced to a source.
